title: Motor Driver: The H-Bridge
description: The controller board can't power a motor directly. This is the part that stands between them — and it's built from exactly four switches.

content.value: Arrange four switches in a diamond shape around a motor, and something clever becomes possible: closing different pairs sends current through the motor in different directions, using the same two wires. That arrangement has a name — an H-bridge, because the wiring diagram of the motor sitting between two pairs of switches looks like the letter H.

content.title: 🔀 Tap the switches
content.hint: Find forward, find reverse, then try closing two switches on the same side.

content.value: Why This Solves the Direction Problem

A motor's terminals aren't labelled forward and reverse — direction only depends on which way current flows through them, as you learned last lesson. Closing switches A and D sends current one way through the motor; closing B and C sends it the other way. Same motor, same two wires, opposite direction, just by choosing a different diagonal pair.

You've also just rediscovered Module 3's short circuit, in a new part: close A and B (or C and D) — both switches on the same side — and you connect the battery's + and − straight to each other with almost nothing in the way. A real motor driver chip is built so its internal circuitry physically can't do that combination; the widget lets you do it anyway so you can see exactly why it's dangerous.
Why Not Just Wire the Controller Straight to the Motor?

You'll meet the full reason in the next lesson, but the short version: a controller pin can only source a tiny trickle of current, nowhere near enough to spin a motor. The four switches in a real motor driver chip aren't hand-flipped like the widget — they're transistors, switched by the controller's weak signal, but each one can pass the motor's much bigger current. The controller decides, the driver does the heavy lifting.

Real driver chips like the L298N or DRV8833 also add PWM control on top of direction — combine what you learned in Module 4 with the H-bridge here, and you get both direction *and* speed from the same four switches.

Key takeaway: an H-bridge is four switches around a motor. Closing a diagonal pair drives it one direction or the other; closing a same-side pair shorts the battery. A real driver chip makes that same-side combination physically impossible.

quiz.question: Which pair of switches, when closed together, drives the motor in the opposite direction from A+D?
quiz.explain: A+D sends current one way; B+C is the other diagonal, sending it the other way through the same motor.

quiz.question: What happens if you close A and B together?
options: A short circuit — the battery's two terminals connect almost directly
quiz.explain: A and B are both on the same side of the diamond, connecting + and − with very little resistance between them — the same failure Module 3 covered, on a new part.

quiz.question: Why can't a controller pin drive a motor directly, without a driver chip?
options: Controller pins can only supply a tiny current, far less than a motor needs
Controller pins don't produce any voltage
quiz.explain: A weak control signal can switch a driver chip's internal transistors, but it can't supply a motor's much larger current on its own — that's exactly what the driver bridges.
